title: Canonical extended-Rees map of a commuting square of closed centres
statement:
Let $V,V',S,S'$ be schemes [def-pc-scheme], let $s:S\hookrightarrow V$ and $s':S'\hookrightarrow V'$ be closed immersions [def-weil-closed-immersion], and let $h:V'\to V$ and $b:S'\to S$ satisfy $h\circ s'=s\circ b$. Write $\mathcal I=\ker(s)$ and $\mathcal I'=\ker(s')$ for their ideal sheaves [def-sbc-closed-immersion-ideal-sheaf]. The ideal-containment conclusion of [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-conormal-functorial] gives $h^{-1}\mathcal I\cdot\mathcal O_{V'}\subseteq\mathcal I'$.

For an ideal sheaf $\mathcal J$ on a scheme $X$, write $D_{\mathcal J}X$ for the actual extended-Rees deformation space: on every affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq X$ with ideal $J=\mathcal J(U)$ its chart is $\operatorname{Spec}R[t,J/t]$, where $R[t,J/t]$ is the subalgebra of $R[t,t^{-1}]$ generated by $R[t]$ and $a/t$ for all $a\in J$. These affine charts and their restriction maps are glued using the spectrum construction [def-weil-affine-spectrum].

Define $\operatorname{pairMap}(s,s',h,b)$ to be the canonical morphism $D_{\mathcal I'}V'\to D_{\mathcal I}V$ obtained as follows. For every affine $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq V$ and $U'=\operatorname{Spec}R'\subseteq V'$ with $U'\subseteq h^{-1}U$, use the existing ideal-map containment for $h^\sharp:R\to R'$ followed by the preceding ideal-containment conclusion to obtain $h^\sharp(\mathcal I(U))R'\subseteq\mathcal I'(U')$. Apply the extended-Rees algebra map $R[t,\mathcal I(U)/t]\to R'[t,\mathcal I'(U')/t]$ with $r\mapsto h^\sharp(r)$, $t\mapsto t$, and $a/t\mapsto h^\sharp(a)/t$, then glue its contravariant spectrum maps. Equivalently this is the existing $\operatorname{deformationSpaceMap}$ with exactly that ideal-containment witness. No conormal-module map is used. The definition applies to every such commuting square, without Noetherian, smoothness, flatness, section, relative-dimension or Cartesian-square assumptions; it includes empty schemes and identity squares. It asserts no base-change or etale-invariance theorem.
